name: Adversarial Statutory Interpretation
title: Adversarial Statutory Interpretation
answer: Adversarial statutory interpretation is the practice of reading a statute from the position of the opposing party, testing how its text, structure and purpose could be turned against the reading a client prefers. In legal research it sits alongside ordinary statutory construction, but its aim is not to find the best reading, it is to find the strongest competing readings before an opponent or a court does. It matters most where a statute is new, sparse or drafted to cover technology that did not exist when it was passed, which is common in AI regulation. The work product is usually a memo mapping each plausible reading to the facts at hand and to the authority that supports it.

sections.body: Adversarial statutory interpretation is the practice of reading a statute from the position of the opposing party, testing how its text, structure and purpose could be turned against the reading a client prefers. In legal research it sits alongside ordinary statutory construction, but its aim is not to find the best reading, it is to find the strongest competing readings before an opponent or a court does. It matters most where a statute is new, sparse or drafted to cover technology that did not exist when it was passed, which is common in AI regulation. The work product is usually a memo mapping each plausible reading to the facts at hand and to the authority that supports it.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the primary sources themselves: statute text, legislative history, regulations, and the case law that has already construed the provision. A researcher typically works from a commercial legal database or a free official source, plus a citator to check whether a case is still good law. Where AI tools are used, they are usually general assistants for summarising or organising text rather than sources of authority, because a citation that cannot be verified is worse than no citation. This site tracks 29 AI case law precedents, a reminder that in the AI field the construing authority is still thin and much of the analysis rests on older statutes applied to new facts.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method starts with the operative words of the statute and the canons of construction: plain meaning, whole text, avoiding surplusage, and reading provisions together rather than in isolation. The researcher then builds the strongest version of the adverse reading, not a straw man, and looks for facts that would make that reading persuasive to a specific judge or agency. Legislative history, purpose clauses and later amendments are checked for support on both sides, and the analysis is tested against how courts have treated similar language in other statutes. The output is a ranked set of readings with the arguments and counterarguments for each, so that strategy can be set before a brief is filed.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The ethical frame is candour: a lawyer may argue a reasonable reading of an ambiguous statute but may not misstate the text or hide controlling authority. Work product and privilege rules govern how the analysis is shared, and a memo written to explore adverse readings is usually kept internal for that reason. Provenance matters when AI tools are involved, since every citation and quotation must be traced to the source and verified before it appears in anything filed. On regulatory questions the same discipline applies to agency guidance and enforcement history, which may signal a reading that the text alone does not. Nothing here is legal advice, and a reader facing a live dispute should work with counsel admitted in the relevant jurisdiction.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The near term is likely to bring more decisions construing older statutes against AI systems, which will gradually convert open questions into settled readings and shrink the space for creative interpretation. As that happens, adversarial reading shifts from guessing at first impression to distinguishing or narrowing precedent, and the value of a well built set of competing readings rises. Legislative drafting may also adapt, with definitions written more tightly to reduce the ambiguity that makes adversarial interpretation productive. Researchers should expect the balance between text, history and purpose to keep moving as courts confront statutes that were never written with these systems in mind.
